Chief Justice Marshall was acknowledging that, in many contexts, 
executive branch decision making represents “the last word” on the 
exercise of government power. Marshall presumably had in mind contexts 
in which the Constitution vests exclusive power in the president—for 
^ample, regarding pardons or his decisions whether and when to negotiate 
treaties with foreign nations. But, as we will explore fiirther in later 
chapters, the executive frequently has the last word also in the context of 
statutory interpretation. On some occasions, this is because Congress has 
decided, m enacting an administrative scheme, to place the executive’s 
exercise of judgment under that scheme beyond judicial review. Kxa Triples 
ateady encountered include the Attorney General’s decisions under the 
Ethics in Government Act whether evidence presented to the Attorney 
General was sufficiently specific to trigger a preliminary investigation 
under the Act and, if so, whether an independent counsel was ultimately 
warranted. Similar examples are common in the exercise of the president’s 
foreign affairs and national security powers, especially because courts may 
be uncertain where the line is to be drawn between constitutionally 
confen’ed and congressionally authorized foreign affairs authorities.
Even when a statute is silent on the question, courts presume that 
Congress does not intend judicial review to be available for executive 
branch decisions not to enforce civil or criminal statutes against particular 
individuals, Heckler v. Chaney, 470 U.S. 821 (1985), or decisions on the 
allocation of expenditures within the general category of any “lump-sum 
appropriation,” Lincoln v. Vigil, 508 U.S. 182 (1993). Yet executive 
decisions to forbear from enforcing particular statutes—or, to put it 
perhaps more accurately, executive decisions as to which statutes will get 
underenforced given limited resources can be powerful drivers of policy. 
Chapter 5 will return to this issue, which has been especially pressing in 
the field of immigration. Nonenforcement has also been a subject of 
controversy with regard to drug enforcement policy, e.g., James M. Cole,
